title: General Pathology
description: Cell injury and death, inflammation and repair, haemodynamic disorders, immunopathology, and neoplasia — the foundation of disease mechanisms.

topics.title: Cell Injury, Adaptation and Cell Death
topics.summary: Cellular adaptations, reversible and irreversible injury, necrosis and apoptosis.

notes.b: Cells adapt to stress by hypertrophy (increase in cell size — cardiac muscle in hypertension), hyperplasia (increase in cell number — endometrium, prostate), atrophy (decrease in size — disuse, denervation) and metaplasia (one adult cell type replaced by another — squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium in smokers; Barrett's oesophagus: squamous → columnar, a precursor of adenocarcinoma). Causes of cell injury include hypoxia (the commonest), physical and chemical agents, infections, immunological reactions, genetic defects and nutritional imbalance. Reversible injury shows cellular swelling (hydropic change) and fatty change; irreversible injury shows membrane damage, mitochondrial dysfunction and nuclear changes (pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis).
k: Hypoxia is the commonest cause of injury

notes.b: Necrosis is uncontrolled cell death with inflammation. Types: coagulative (most solid organs after ischaemia, e.g. myocardial infarction — architecture preserved), liquefactive (brain infarcts and abscesses), caseous (tuberculosis — cheese-like, with granulomas), fat necrosis (acute pancreatitis, breast trauma — chalky saponification), fibrinoid (vessel walls in malignant hypertension and vasculitis) and gangrenous (dry, wet, gas gangrene). Apoptosis is programmed, energy-dependent cell death without inflammation: cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, apoptotic bodies phagocytosed; mediated by caspases through intrinsic (mitochondrial, cytochrome c; regulated by BCL-2 family) and extrinsic (death receptor — Fas, TNF) pathways. It occurs physiologically (embryogenesis, hormone withdrawal) and pathologically (viral infection, DNA damage).

topics.title: Acute and Chronic Inflammation
topics.summary: Vascular and cellular events, mediators, outcomes, chronic and granulomatous inflammation.

notes.b: Acute inflammation is a rapid response to injury or infection with cardinal signs: rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling), dolor (pain) and functio laesa (loss of function). Vascular events: transient vasoconstriction, vasodilatation, increased permeability (exudate rich in protein), and stasis. Cellular events: margination, rolling (selectins), adhesion (integrins), transmigration (diapedesis) and chemotaxis of neutrophils (the first cells, within 6–24 hours), followed by phagocytosis and killing (oxygen-dependent myeloperoxidase system). Mediators: histamine (immediate permeability), prostaglandins (pain, fever, vasodilatation — blocked by NSAIDs), leukotrienes (bronchoconstriction, chemotaxis — LTB4), bradykinin (pain), complement (C3a, C5a anaphylatoxins; C5a chemotaxis; C3b opsonin), cytokines (IL-1, TNF, IL-6 — fever and acute-phase response). Outcomes: resolution, abscess, healing by fibrosis, or chronic inflammation.

Chronic inflammation is prolonged inflammation with simultaneous tissue destruction and repair, dominated by macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells, with angiogenesis and fibrosis. Causes: persistent infection (TB, leprosy, syphilis), prolonged exposure to toxins (silica), and autoimmunity (rheumatoid arthritis). Granulomatous inflammation is a special type with granulomas — collections of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with Langhans giant cells (horseshoe nuclei), surrounded by lymphocytes; caseating granulomas suggest TB, non-caseating suggest sarcoidosis. Other granulomatous causes: leprosy, schistosomiasis, fungal infections, foreign bodies, Crohn's disease. Systemic effects of inflammation: fever, leucocytosis, raised ESR and CRP, and the acute-phase response.

topics.title: Tissue Repair and Haemodynamic Disorders
topics.summary: Regeneration and fibrosis, wound healing, oedema, thrombosis, embolism, infarction and shock.

notes.b: Tissues are labile (continuously dividing — skin, gut epithelium, bone marrow), stable (quiescent but can divide — liver, kidney tubules) or permanent (non-dividing — neurons, cardiac muscle, which heal by scarring). Repair involves regeneration and/or fibrosis with granulation tissue (new capillaries, fibroblasts, inflammatory cells). Collagen type III is laid down first and replaced by type I. Complications: keloids (excess collagen extending beyond the wound, common in people of African descent), hypertrophic scars, contractures, and wound dehiscence. Healing is impaired by infection, poor nutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), diabetes, steroids and poor blood supply.
k: Keloids more common in people of African descent

notes.b: Virchow's triad of thrombosis: endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence) and hypercoagulability. Deep vein thrombosis commonly embolises to the lungs (pulmonary embolism). Emboli may be thrombotic (most common), fat (after long-bone fractures), air, amniotic fluid, tumour or septic. An infarct is ischaemic necrosis: pale (white) infarcts occur in solid organs with end-arterial supply (heart, kidney, spleen); red (haemorrhagic) infarcts occur in organs with dual supply or loose tissue (lung, intestine) and with venous occlusion. Oedema results from raised hydrostatic pressure, reduced oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction or increased permeability. Shock (hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive — septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic — and obstructive) causes inadequate tissue perfusion.
k: Pale infarcts: heart, kidney; red: lung, bowel

topics.title: Immunopathology
topics.summary: Hypersensitivity reactions, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency and amyloidosis.

notes.b: Gell and Coombs classification: Type I (immediate, IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation — anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, asthma, urticaria); Type II (antibody-mediated cytotoxic — against cell or matrix antigens: transfusion reactions, haemolytic disease of the newborn, Goodpasture's syndrome, myasthenia gravis, Graves' disease); Type III (immune complex deposition — post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, SLE, serum sickness, Arthus reaction); Type IV (delayed, T-cell mediated, 48–72 hours — tuberculin (Mantoux) test, contact dermatitis, TB granulomas, transplant rejection).
k: Type II: antibody against cells — transfusion reaction
Type III: immune complexes — SLE, PSGN
Type IV: T cells — Mantoux, contact dermatitis

notes.b: Autoimmune diseases result from loss of self-tolerance: organ-specific (type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, myasthenia gravis) or systemic (SLE — antinuclear and anti-dsDNA antibodies; rheumatoid arthritis — rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP). Immunodeficiencies are primary (e.g. X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, DiGeorge syndrome, severe combined immunodeficiency) or secondary — most commonly HIV infection (CD4 T-cell depletion; AIDS when CD4 < 200 cells/µL or an AIDS-defining illness), malnutrition, malignancy and immunosuppressive drugs. Amyloidosis is extracellular deposition of misfolded fibrillar protein (β-pleated sheets): AL (light chains — myeloma), AA (serum amyloid A — chronic inflammation such as TB, rheumatoid arthritis), Aβ (Alzheimer's disease); it stains with Congo red showing apple-green birefringence.

q: Anaphylaxis is a Type ___ hypersensitivity reaction.
The Mantoux (tuberculin) skin test is an example of Type ___ hypersensitivity.
Delayed-type hypersensitivity mediated by T cells, read at 48–72 hours.
An ABO-incompatible blood transfusion reaction is Type ___ hypersensitivity.
Antibodies bind antigens on red cells.
Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are characteristic of:
Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE.
The most common cause of acquired immunodeficiency worldwide is:
Amyloid is identified in tissue by Congo red staining showing:
Chronic inflammatory diseases such as TB and rheumatoid arthritis
Serum amyloid A rises in chronic inflammation.

topics.title: Neoplasia
topics.summary: Benign versus malignant tumours, carcinogenesis, oncogenes, spread, grading and staging, and tumour markers.

notes.b: A neoplasm is an abnormal mass of tissue whose growth exceeds and is uncoordinated with normal tissue and persists after the stimulus stops. Benign tumours are well differentiated, slow-growing, encapsulated, non-invasive and do not metastasise (e.g. lipoma, fibroadenoma, leiomyoma/fibroid — very common in Nigerian women). Malignant tumours show anaplasia (lack of differentiation, pleomorphism, high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, abnormal mitoses), invasion and metastasis. Carcinomas arise from epithelium (spread via lymphatics), sarcomas from mesenchyme (spread via blood). Dysplasia is disordered growth; carcinoma in situ has not breached the basement membrane. Routes of spread: local invasion, lymphatic, haematogenous and transcoelomic (e.g. ovarian cancer in the peritoneum).
k: Carcinoma in situ: basement membrane intact

notes.b: Carcinogenesis is multistep accumulation of genetic changes: activation of oncogenes (e.g. RAS, MYC, HER2) and inactivation of tumour suppressor genes (TP53, RB — Knudson's two-hit hypothesis), plus defects in DNA repair and apoptosis. Carcinogens: chemical (tobacco smoke — lung, bladder; aflatoxin — liver), physical (UV — skin; ionising radiation) and biological — oncogenic viruses important in Nigeria: HPV (cervical cancer — the second commonest cancer in Nigerian women after breast), hepatitis B and C (hepatocellular carcinoma), EBV (Burkitt lymphoma — endemic in malarial belts; nasopharyngeal carcinoma), HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma in HIV), and Schistosoma haematobium (squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder). Grading describes differentiation (histology); staging describes extent of spread (TNM: tumour size, nodes, metastasis) and is more important for prognosis. Tumour markers: AFP (hepatocellular carcinoma, germ-cell tumours), PSA (prostate), CA-125 (ovary), CEA (colorectal), β-hCG (choriocarcinoma).

q: A key feature distinguishing malignant from benign tumours is:
Sarcomas characteristically spread via the bloodstream.
Carcinoma in situ is defined by:
Malignant cells not yet breaching the basement membrane
It has not invaded underlying tissue.
The virus most strongly linked to cervical cancer is:

The most important determinant of cancer prognosis is usually:
